parts.text: Over the past few days, I have been studying Anthropic's work, published this July, on visualizing a model's global workspace. I found it very inspiring, so I wanted to write down my understanding and thoughts.

parts.text: Abstract

blocks.text: Abstract

parts.text: This note uses a theater analogy to introduce the global workspace, leading into the central idea of Anthropic's article: how can we observe a large language model's "global workspace"? We will first look at how their tools for observing and intervening on intermediate representations, J-Lens and J-Space, work. Then we will see how the researchers use these tools and their experiments to argue that large language models may have a global workspace, and to explore some of its interesting properties. Finally, I will share some of my own thoughts and questions about the article.

blocks.text: Global Workspace Theory

parts.text: In the gorilla experiment, the visual input clearly includes the pixels of the gorilla, and these pixels are processed by the visual cortex. Yet they are not captured by awareness. The experiment gives us a simple demonstration that not every signal enters consciousness. So how does the brain process information? This was one of the puzzles facing cognitive science.

The experiment gives us a simple demonstration that not every signal enters consciousness. So how does the brain process information? This was one of the puzzles facing cognitive science.

parts.text: To address this question, Bernard Baars proposed one possible explanation: Global Workspace Theory (GWT, Baars, 1988).

blocks.text: To address this question, Bernard Baars proposed one possible explanation: Global Workspace Theory (GWT, Baars, 1988).

parts.text: The theory gives us a vivid picture. The whole cognitive system is like a large theater, and the central stage is the global workspace. The props and actors on this stage are the things we can consciously perceive. Of course, this is a very unusual theater: it is a cognitive system, after all! The audience surrounding the stage corresponds to the brain circuits that specialize in different kinds of information processing.

The whole cognitive system is like a large theater, and the central stage is the global workspace. **The props and actors on this stage are the things we can consciously perceive.** Of course, this is a very unusual theater: it is a cognitive system, after all! The audience surrounding the stage corresponds to the brain circuits that specialize in different kinds of information processing.

emphasis.source: The props and actors on this stage are the things we can consciously perceive.

parts.text: Our brains constantly process information from the body: the smell of a pleasant fragrance, the touch of keys under our fingers, the sight of a leaf's texture, the sound of someone shouting by the road, or the subtle taste of tea. Various small circuits or functions process this information, which competes for a place on the stage.

parts.text: Imagine these circuits as skilled makeup artists preparing aspiring actors who run along the central avenue into the theater. Returning to the invisible gorilla experiment, some applicants never even get through the door, such as things outside the screen. Some look like natural stars, such as the players in white. There are also many supporting performers, such as the players in black, and others who enter the theater but never make it onto the stage, such as the gorilla.

parts.text: The makeup artists, our small brain processors, prepare the actors one by one. The applicants move through successive stages of this production line. By the time they reach the stage, they have gone from an unadorned appearance to smart suits and full makeup. If the stage selector thinks an actor stands out, they are allowed onstage. Those who are too inconspicuous may be turned away.

Once onstage, these actors become objects that consciousness can observe and manipulate, through reasoning, translation, or rotation.

parts.text: What makes this a global workspace is broadcasting: once information enters the stage, multiple specialized processing systems around it can read and use it together. These systems handle not only external sensory input, but also memory, reasoning, decision-making, and language.

blocks.text: What makes this a *global* workspace is **broadcasting**: once information enters the stage, multiple specialized processing systems around it can read and use it together. These systems handle not only external sensory input, but also memory, reasoning, decision-making, and language.

parts.text: For example, seeing dark clouds over a mountain might remind the memory system of getting caught in the rain, prompt the decision-making system to consider heading downhill, and let the language system form the sentence, "It might rain." Reaching the stage therefore means both entering awareness and becoming available for flexible use by multiple systems.

parts.text: A Global Workspace in Large Language Models? J-Lens and J-Space

blocks.text: A Global Workspace in Large Language Models? J-Lens and J-Space

parts.text: The central idea of the J-Space article is that large language models may have something resembling a global workspace, or GW. How could we establish that such a workspace exists in a model? It would lie somewhere in the successive Transformer blocks, but how could we argue that these hard-to-interpret intermediate layers constitute a GW?

blocks.text: The central idea of the J-Space article is that large language models may have something resembling a global workspace, or GW. How could we establish that such a workspace exists in a model? It would lie somewhere in the successive Transformer blocks, but how could we argue that these hard-to-interpret intermediate layers constitute a GW?

parts.text: The article introduces two concepts: J-Lens and J-Space.

blocks.text: The article introduces two concepts: J-Lens and J-Space.

parts.text: J-Lens lets us examine the state of a model's GW at a particular moment. J-Space gives a mathematical definition of a state space formed by the representations this method can read. We can think of it as an approximate, readable state space of the GW. I will introduce them one by one.

blocks.text: J-Lens lets us examine the state of a model's GW at a particular moment. J-Space gives a mathematical definition of a state space formed by the representations this method can read. We can think of it as an **approximate, readable state space** of the GW. I will introduce them one by one.

parts.text: There is one caveat here. This word distribution cannot directly be treated as the probability that the model believes a particular claim; rather, we can intuitively think of it as how likely a word is to represent a concept, or actor, being considered in this layer's workspace. That wording is not entirely precise, but it offers an intuitive way to think about it. For instance, reading out spider tells us that a spider-related concept is present. The model might be considering spider as the answer, ruling it out, or comparing spiders with ants. The word alone does not distinguish these possibilities. parts.text: My main questions about this method concern J-Space.

parts.text: First, we should distinguish two possible forms of non-uniqueness. The J-Lens vectors form an overcomplete dictionary, so the same vector may admit several coefficient sets. Meanwhile, J-Space under a sparsity constraint is generally nonconvex, so a given hidden state may also have more than one nearest point. These are different issues, and nonconvexity alone does not imply that every hidden state has multiple optimal decompositions. What concerns me more is whether the sparse decomposition of the same hidden state is stable.
